theme: Elijah taken up; Elisha receives the mantle
readingInstruction: Read 2 Kings 1:1-2:25. Elijah’s ministry ends in a whirlwind, and Elisha takes up his mantle. Notice the careful details about the crossing of the Jordan and the request for a double portion.
settingTheScene: The book of 2 Kings begins where 1 Kings ended, with Ahab’s death and his son Ahaziah on the throne. Elijah’s final acts include a confrontation over consulting a foreign god. Then the narrative turns to the transition from Elijah to Elisha, one of the most dramatic passages in the Old Testament. The crossing of the Jordan recalls Joshua and the exodus.
observation: Ahaziah sends messengers to inquire of Baal-zebub, and Elijah says, “Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are going to inquire of Baal-zebub?” (1:3).
Fire falls from heaven on two companies of fifty, but the third captain pleads for his life (1:9-15).
Elijah and Elisha cross the Jordan on dry ground when Elijah strikes the water with his cloak (2:8).
Elisha says, “Please let there be a double portion of your spirit on me” (2:9).
“And behold, chariots of fire and horses of fire separated the two of them. And Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven” (2:11).
Elisha cries, “My father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!” (2:12).
Elisha takes up Elijah’s cloak and asks, “Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?” and strikes the water, and it parts (2:13-14).
The sons of the prophets say, “The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha” (2:15).
interpretation:
Chapter 1 shows once again the foolishness of seeking help from other gods. Ahaziah is ill and sends to Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron. The question Elijah asks is blunt: “Is it because there is no God in Israel?” It is a rebuke to all who treat the true God as one option among many. The fire episode is dramatic and shows the seriousness of opposing God’s prophet. The third captain’s humble approach is the one that finds mercy.

Chapter 2 is the high point. Elijah is about to be taken, and Elisha will not leave him. Three times Elijah tells him to stay behind, and three times Elisha refuses. His loyalty and persistence are remarkable. When Elijah asks what he can do for him, Elisha does not ask for wealth or safety. He asks for a double portion of Elijah’s spirit, the share of the firstborn son. He wants to be Elijah’s heir and to continue his ministry.

The departure of Elijah is one of two times in the Old Testament that someone is taken to heaven without dying (the other is Enoch). Chariots and horses of fire appear, a vision of the heavenly army. Elisha’s cry, “My father, my father!” acknowledges Elijah as a spiritual father and as Israel’s real defense. The chariots of Israel are not its armies but its prophets.

Then Elisha takes the cloak, steps to the Jordan, and asks the question that sums up the whole passage: “Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?” The prophet is gone, but God remains. The waters part. Elisha is not Elijah, but the same God is with him.

The chapter ends with a hard episode: boys mock Elisha and are attacked by bears. This is not about baldness. It is about contempt for God’s prophet, and the seriousness of mocking God’s word.
connection: John the Baptist came in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17). Jesus ascended into heaven, taken up before the eyes of his disciples (Acts 1:9-11), and sent the Spirit on them. The “double portion” finds its fulfillment at Pentecost. Hebrews 2:2-4 warns against ignoring a greater salvation. Jesus crossed from death to life and opened the way for all his people.
application:
Ask whether you want a double portion of God’s Spirit, and what you would do with it.

Practice Elisha’s persistence in following a spiritual mentor.

When someone you depend on is taken from you, ask, “Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?” and trust that he remains.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to give you a hunger for his Spirit.
Thank him that he remains when those who guide you are gone.
Ask him to keep you from mocking what he sends.
